name: italian tomato sauces
instructions:
Four italian tomato-sauce shapes under one roof.

- VARIANT A — MARCELLA HAZAN'S 3-INGREDIENT TOMATO SAUCE
- VARIANT B — SICILIAN TOMATO PESTO (pesto rosso alla trapanese; raw blended pesto)
- VARIANT C — VODKA SAUCE (tomato-and-cream outlier)
- VARIANT D — PIPERADE (blended vegetable-tomato base)

=== VARIANT A — MARCELLA HAZAN'S 3-INGREDIENT TOMATO SAUCE ===

Marcella Hazan's famous three-ingredient sauce. The simplest possible italian tomato sauce; canonical starting point.

INGREDIENTS:
- 28-oz can whole peeled tomatoes (San Marzano ideal — canned whole, not diced, not paste)
- 1 medium yellow onion, peeled and halved (NOT chopped — kept in halves)
- 5 tablespoons unsalted butter
- salt to taste

PROCEDURE:
1. Combine tomatoes, butter, onion halves, and a pinch of salt in a saucepan.
2. Simmer uncovered on low for ~45 minutes, stirring occasionally and crushing the tomatoes with the back of a spoon as they soften.
3. Fish out and discard the onion halves before serving (they've done their aromatic job).
4. Toss with cooked pasta.

=== VARIANT B — TRADITIONAL SICILIAN TOMATO PESTO (PESTO ROSSO ALLA TRAPANESE) ===

The full canonical form. No cooking — a raw blended pesto.

INGREDIENTS:
- sun-dried tomatoes (rehydrated in warm water if dry-packed; drain and pat dry)
- almonds (blanched, unsalted)
- fresh basil leaves
- garlic (raw, 1-2 cloves)
- olive oil (good quality)
- pecorino cheese (traditional) or parmesan cheese
- salt
- red chili flakes (optional, traditional in some sicilian versions)
- pasta (short shapes like busiate traditionally; penne, fusilli, or trofie all work)

PROCEDURE:
1. Rehydrate the sun-dried tomatoes if dry-packed. Skip if oil-packed.
2. In a food processor or blender, combine sun-dried tomatoes, almonds, basil, garlic, and a pinch of red chili flakes. Pulse to a rough paste.
3. With the motor running, drizzle in olive oil until the sauce reaches a thick, spreadable consistency — a loose paste, not a smooth sauce.
4. Fold in grated pecorino (or parmesan) and salt to taste. Fold in by hand off the blades — don't blend the cheese.
5. Toss with hot cooked pasta. Loosen with a splash of pasta water if too thick.

=== VARIANT C — VODKA SAUCE (GIGI HADID STYLE) ===

A DIFFERENT BRANCH of the tomato family — this one adds heavy cream. Structurally it belongs somewhere between the pure-tomato family (tomato base, cooked) and a cream sauce. It's here because the sauce is fundamentally a tomato dish that happens to add cream, not a cream dish that happens to add tomato.

INGREDIENTS:
- 1 medium yellow onion, finely chopped
- 3-4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2-3 tablespoons butter
- 2-3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4-6 tablespoons tomato paste (concentrated)
- 1/4 cup vodka
- 1/2 to 3/4 cup heavy whipping cream
- red chili flakes (canonical here — the gigi hadid version leans on them)
- grated parmesan cheese
- fresh basil (torn, off heat)
- salt to taste
- pasta (short shapes — penne, rigatoni)

PROCEDURE:
1. Sauté onion and garlic in butter + olive oil until softened.
2. Add tomato paste and cook it hard in the fat until it darkens a shade and smells sweet-caramelized (~3-5 min). This is the load-bearing flavor step.
3. Pour in vodka; let it reduce briefly (~2 min).
4. Stir in heavy cream and red chili flakes. Simmer to combine.
5. Off heat, fold in grated parmesan and torn fresh basil. Salt to taste.
6. Toss with cooked short pasta.

=== VARIANT D — PIPERADE ===

A sautéed-and-blended vegetable-and-tomato sauce. Same underlying technique as the piperade in ratatouille variant B, but with additions that push it toward pasta-sauce territory (see notes on how this differs from the ratatouille version).

INGREDIENTS:
- 1 medium yellow onion, roughly chopped
- 1-2 bell peppers, roughly chopped
- 1-2 carrots, roughly chopped
- 3-4 cloves garlic
- tomatoes (canned whole peeled or fresh — both work; sauce gets blended smooth)
- olive oil
- salt to taste
- pasta (short shapes; long-cut also fine since this blends smooth)

PICK-ANY-ONE-OR-MORE FOR PASTA SAVORINESS (see PIPERADE VS RATATOUILLE note):
- tomato paste (a spoonful, cooked into the base for depth)
- heavy cream (a splash near the end)
- butter (a knob mounted in off heat)
- light miso paste (small amount, adds fermented depth)

PROCEDURE:
1. Sauté the chopped onion + bell pepper + carrot + garlic in olive oil until softened and starting to caramelize.
2. Add tomatoes; simmer to cook down (~15-20 min).
3. Add any of the savoriness options (tomato paste, cream, butter, miso).
4. Blend smooth (immersion blender in the pot, or transfer to a countertop blender).
5. Salt to taste. Toss with cooked pasta.

=== SIBLING RECIPES (SEE NOTES FOR PLACEMENT RULES) ===

- italian-green-sauce-and-pesto: the green-sauce / basil-pesto side of the family.
- bolognese: the protein-forward, long-simmered, cutting-board-cut side of the italian pasta family. See DIFFERENTIATION FROM THE RAGU FAMILY note.
- mushroom-eggplant-ragu, fire-roasted-meatballs: also in the ragu family; not tomato-sauce shape.
notes:
=== VARIANT A NOTES — MARCELLA'S 3-INGREDIENT TOMATO SAUCE ===

WHY IT WORKS WITH ONLY THREE INGREDIENTS: Hazan's insight is that a whole peeled canned tomato + butter + onion, given enough time (~45 min uncovered), builds a sauce that reads more complex than the ingredient list suggests. Butter adds richness and rounds acidity in a way olive oil can't at this simplicity. The onion halves perfume the sauce without becoming a chunky component — that's why they go in whole and come out before serving. No garlic, no basil, no oregano, no chili — the restraint is the recipe.

DON'T CHOP THE ONION: the onion halves are meant to be discarded. Chopping the onion turns it into part of the sauce texture and changes the dish.

UNSALTED BUTTER, GENEROUS: Hazan calls for 5 tablespoons per 28-oz can. Don't cut it — the butter is doing structural work, not just flavor. Unsalted so you control the seasoning.

SAN MARZANO IF POSSIBLE: whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes are what the recipe was tuned to. Other whole peeled canned tomatoes work; diced canned tomatoes read watery here.

=== VARIANT B NOTES — SICILIAN TOMATO PESTO ===

SUN-DRIED TOMATOES ARE THE STRUCTURAL INGREDIENT — NOT TOMATO PASTE, NOT CANNED: the tomato base for variant B is specifically sun-dried tomatoes. Their chewy, umami-forward, slightly sweet dried-fruit register is what makes this read as pesto rather than sauce. Tomato paste is too cooked/concentrated; canned tomatoes carry too much water for a raw blended paste.

ALMONDS ARE THE NUT — BLANCHED, UNSALTED: pine nuts are for green pesto; almonds anchor red. Blanched (skins off) gives the cleanest color. Unsalted so you control the seasoning.

PINE NUTS ARE CLASHING — DIFFERENT PESTO ENTIRELY: pine nuts belong in green pesto (see italian-green-sauce-and-pesto) where their delicate resiny sweetness bridges basil and parmesan. In a tomato base they get lost.

BASIL IS NON-OPTIONAL IN VARIANT B: without fresh basil the dish reads underwhelming — just ground sun-dried tomatoes and almonds with cheese. Basil is what makes it a pesto rather than an italian-tomato-and-almond spread.

PECORINO IS TRADITIONAL; PARMESAN IS FINE: the classic sicilian version uses pecorino — sharper, saltier, sheep's-milk depth against the sweet sun-dried tomatoes. Parmesan works too and is more likely to be on hand; pecorino is the upgrade when you have it.

FOOD PROCESSOR OR BLENDER, NOT MORTAR: red pesto wants a blender or food processor. Almonds are too hard to break down by hand with a pestle in reasonable time. Green pesto is a mortar dish; red pesto is a blender dish.

SHORT PASTA SHAPES: sicilian tradition pairs pesto trapanese with busiate (a twisted pasta). Penne, fusilli, trofie, cavatelli, or orecchiette all work. Long strands (spaghetti, linguine) don't grip red pesto well.

=== VARIANT C NOTES — VODKA SAUCE (DIFFERENT BRANCH — TOMATO + CREAM) ===

VARIANT C SITS ON A DIFFERENT BRANCH: vodka sauce is the outlier in the family. Variants A/B stay on the pure-tomato axis (with almonds+cheese carrying fat load in B); C adds heavy cream and moves the sauce toward a cross-family space between italian tomato and cream sauces. That's why the placement note calls it 'a different branch.' It still belongs in this file because the tomato paste + tomato register is doing the flavor work — this is a tomato sauce that happens to add cream, not a cream sauce that happens to add tomato.

TOMATO PASTE IS THE TOMATO SOURCE — LOAD-BEARING: variant C uses tomato PASTE cooked hard in the fat until it darkens as the main tomato base. This is opposite of variants A and B (which want canned whole tomatoes or sun-dried respectively). Paste is structural for C, clashing for A/B.

=== VARIANT D NOTES — PIPERADE ===

CORE INGREDIENTS: onion + bell pepper + tomato + carrot + garlic sautéed and blended smooth. That's the whole thing. Everything else in the ingredient list is a savoriness option (see next note).

PIPERADE VS RATATOUILLE PIPERADE — SAME BASE, DIFFERENT ADDITIONS: this variant IS structurally the same sauce as the piperade in ratatouille variant B. Both are onion + bell pepper + carrot + tomato + garlic sautéed and blended smooth.

The difference: THIS ONE (pasta piperade) often takes SAVORINESS ADDITIONS to make it richer and pasta-appropriate:
- TOMATO PASTE for depth
- HEAVY CREAM for body
- BUTTER for richness
- LIGHT MISO PASTE for fermented depth

Ratatouille's piperade is the bed for a vegetable tian and stays cleaner (no dairy, no miso, no paste beyond a spoonful) so the tianed vegetables lead. This one is the sauce that COATS pasta, so it can take more richness without being upstaged.

Pick any one or more of the savoriness additions based on what you want. All work.

WALNUTS / NUTRITIONAL YEAST / RED CHILI FLAKES WERE HERE AS IMPROVISATIONAL ADDS — REMOVED: earlier versions of this variant listed a few walnuts, nutritional yeast, and red chili flakes as part of the ingredient list. Removed — they're improvisational tools, not part of the core piperade identity. If you want to add them, do; but they don't need to live in the ingredient list. Same principle applies to any other improvised add.

BLEND SMOOTH — SAUCE, NOT CHUNKY: the whole point of the sauté-and-blend format is a smooth sauce. Immersion blender in the pot is easiest; countertop blender works too. Chunky texture pushes the sauce into a stewed-vegetables register, which isn't the target.


=== IF YOU IMPROVISE WITH NUTS — TOASTED WALNUTS OR PEELED ALMONDS ===

If you're adding nuts as an improv here (any variant), TOASTED WALNUTS or PEELED ALMONDS are best. Both fit the tomato-sauce register cleanly.

- PINE NUTS + SUNFLOWER SEEDS: green-pesto territory, not this. Pine nuts stay clashing across this file.
- CASHEWS: better in cream-forward dishes (see chocolate-ganache, spinach-ricotta variant B). Don't reach for them in a tomato base.

=== SHARED / CROSS-VARIANT NOTES ===

TOMATO PASTE PLACEMENT: variants A and B don't want tomato paste — A wants canned whole tomatoes, B wants sun-dried. Paste's concentrated cooked-canned character reads wrong. Variants C (vodka) and D (piperade) both take tomato paste, but for different roles — structural in C (the tomato source), enrichment in D (a savoriness add on top of fresh/canned tomatoes).

SUNFLOWER SEEDS ARE CLASHING — CHALKY IN RED SAUCES: sunflower seeds work in green pesto but read CHALKY in red / tomato sauces. Tested and confirmed. Stick with almonds for variant B; skip sunflower seeds entirely.

SHORT PASTA SHAPES ACROSS THE BOARD: A, B, C generally prefer short shapes (penne, fusilli, rigatoni, trofie) over long strands. The sauces are thick or chunky enough that spaghetti/linguine slide out from under them. Variant D (piperade, blended smooth) is more forgiving — long cuts also work there.

=== DIFFERENTIATION FROM THE RAGU FAMILY — WHAT'S NOT HERE ===

This file is deliberately narrow — protein-free tomato sauces and pesti that are either whole-or-blended (never knife-diced into discrete chunks). Everything that lives on the OTHER side of these axes belongs in the ragu family (three files: bolognese, mushroom-eggplant-ragu, fire-roasted-meatballs):

- PROTEIN-FORWARD: any variant with a meat / faux-meat / lentil slot doing structural work belongs in the ragu family. Nuts and cheese fill the fat-and-protein slot here; that's the tell.
- SLOW-SIMMERED (3+ HOURS): Marcella's bolognese needs its long uncovered simmer to become itself. This file maxes out at ~45 min (Hazan's A); the sicilian pesto B is raw. A 3-hour cook doesn't fit here.
- WHOLE-OR-BLENDED, NOT KNIFE-DICED: ragu's soffrito stays visible in the finished dish. Here, Hazan halves the onion and discards it (no dicing at all); B and D go into a blender; C is finely diced but cooked down entirely into the sauce. No discrete chunks survive.
- MAIN-DISH SAUCE ROLE: ragu is the main event with pasta as delivery vehicle. Tomato sauces here are pasta-finishers — pasta and sauce as equal partners.
original_chef: Variant A: Marcella Hazan (3-ingredient tomato sauce, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking). Variants B-D: mine (sicilian pesto rosso is classical / traditional; not one specific author).
